newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British rates may rise as retail sales surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British rates may rise as retail sales surge.

text.p: British consumer spending showed robust growth in April and the country's leading business organisation said interest rates would continue rising to stop inflation getting out of hand.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail sales rose a seasonally adjusted 0.1 percent in April, giving an annual growth rate of 4.7 percent compared with 4.4 percent in March.

Economists said the Bank of England, newly empowered by the Labour government to set monetary policy, was likely to view the figures as further evidence that economic growth needed to be checked by higher interest rates.

The ONS revised down its estimates of growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the first quarter to 0.9 percent from the initial figure of 1.0 percent, but left the annual rate unchanged at 3.0 percent.

"Despite the downward revision to GDP estimates in the first quarter of the year, growth remains too strong to be sustained indefinitely without triggering inflationary pressures," said Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS.
The Confederation of British industry (CBI) predicted robust growth over the next two years, with GDP likely to average 3.1 percent in 1997 and 2.7 percent in 1998.
"The buoyant outlook largely reflects higher consumer spending growth due to higher real incomes and greater windfall gains than previously assumed," it said.
The CBI was referring to the generous pay-outs millions of Britons will receive when some mutually owned building societies and insurance companies are floated on the stock exchange this year.
"In contrast, weaker export growth than last year is still expected due to the strength of sterling," the CBI added.
It expects official interest rates, now 6.25 percent, to rise to 6.75 percent by the end of the year and seven percent next year.
The CBI's industrial trends survey for May showed demand for British manufactured goods remained weak, with export demand in particular at its lowest level since November 1993.

"Our survey shows that the strength of sterling is continuing to take its toll on manufacturers' ability to win export orders," said Sudhir Junankar, associate director of economic analysis at the CBI.

Garrard of UBS said the day's figures confirmed that the economy was suffering from a "split personality", with a buoyant consumer sector struggling to compensate for weakness in manufacturing, largely due to the strong pound.
He and other economists expect new Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown to raise taxes in a mini-budget in June or July to dampen consumer demand.
This would reduce pressure on the Bank of England's new Monetary Policy Committee to push interest rates up further.

"Policy will have to be tightened and if Mr Brown does not raise taxes, the monetary policy committee will not hesitate to raise interest rates," said Geoffrey Dicks of NatWest Markets. "The ball is in the chancellor's court."
